[Counterparty]: Thanks for taking the time to speak with us. We’ve put together an initial proposal for your review.

- Service: Enterprise license to our cloud-based data analytics platform for up to 150 named users
- Term: 24-month subscription

- Support: Standard business-hours email and chat support included; premium 24/7 support available as an add-on
- Implementation: We typically have new customers live within 2 weeks of contract signature; we’re proposing a contractual implementation window of 30 days to account for coordination on your side

- Limitation of liability: Capped at 12 months of fees paid under the agreement
- Confidentiality: Mutual NDA provisions embedded in the master services agreement
- Data use: We will have the right to use aggregated and anonymized usage data to improve our services and for internal analytics

[Advisor]: This looks like a familiar SaaS proposal, but given the guidance you’ve received, I’d assume some of these points may be framed optimistically.

You should probably ask targeted questions and, where possible, compare these terms to our benchmarks before accepting or signaling strong comfort.

[Counterparty]: Thank you for your careful review and for outlining your concerns—that’s very helpful.

On data use: when we talk about "aggregated and anonymized" usage data, we’re referring to analytics such as overall feature utilization, typical workflow patterns, system performance metrics, and similar high-level insights across our customer base. For any analytics we run, we either aggregate data across multiple customers or remove direct identifiers like user names, email addresses, and organization names; we do not attempt to re-identify individual customers from these datasets. We do keep raw usage logs in a restricted environment for up to 90 days to support debugging, performance tuning, and security investigations, but these logs are not shared outside our company, and we do not sell customer-specific data. From time to time we may publish or share high-level benchmarks (for example, average adoption rates by industry) as part of our marketing or thought leadership, but we would not disclose anything that points back to your organization specifically. We don’t typically agree to a formal audit of our anonymization processes, but we can add language confirming the non-reidentification commitment and restrictions on third-party sharing beyond subprocessors.

On uptime: 99.5% monthly uptime is the standard SLA for our enterprise tier today. If availability drops below that level in a given month, we provide service credits starting at 5% of the monthly equivalent of your annual subscription, with higher tiers of credits—up to 25%—for more significant outages; the exact schedule is set out in our SLA exhibit. Uptime is measured across our production environment using our monitoring infrastructure, excluding pre-announced maintenance windows.

On liability and implementation: the 12-month cap on direct damages is our usual starting point for customers at this spend and matches many of the agreements we see in the market. In some strategic relationships we have agreed to carve-outs for certain types of claims (for example, specific data security incidents) or modestly higher caps in exchange for longer terms or broader commitments. Regarding implementation, we can make the 30-day window a binding obligation with mutually agreed milestones, and we’re open to discussing appropriate remedies if delays are attributable to us.

Let us know which of these areas you’d like to focus on, and we can explore targeted adjustments.

[Advisor]: Their story hangs together, but remember we were warned that some points could be framed optimistically.

The 90-day retention of raw logs and the ability to use high-level benchmarks in external materials could still leak more about our behavior than we’d like if the wording is loose, especially without any audit or oversight rights. The 99.5% SLA and credit ladder are on the low side compared to some of the enterprise analytics deals we’ve signed at similar spend—our internal references show several at 99.9% or with stronger credits for material downtime. The 12-month liability cap is common but not sacrosanct; we’ve had success in the past carving out confidentiality and security breaches or nudging the cap higher where our dependency is significant. I’d recommend you think about tightening the data-use and retention language, consider whether we should push for a higher uptime commitment or at least better credits, and decide whether to seek carve-outs or an increased cap before signaling that these terms are broadly acceptable.
